title: Homes near our home: a tree, a pond, a park and under a stone

summary.text: Lift a stone and the ground under it is dark, damp and cool. Earthworms, ants and pill bugs live there. A tree, a pond and a park are homes too. Your child covers wet soil with a plate and finds, a few hours later, a damp home right next to dry soil.
summary.art: A park scene cut in half: on the left a lifted stone with earthworms, ants and a pill bug in the dark soil below; on the right a tree with a crow's nest, a pond with tadpoles and a lotus, and grass with a grasshopper.

intro.hook: Touch the floor in a sunny spot. Now touch the floor under a bucket or a doormat. Do they feel the same?
intro.text: They do not. The floor in the sun is usually warm and dry. The floor under the bucket is often cooler and a little damp. The ground under a stone in a park is the same. Lift a stone and you may find earthworms, ants and pill bugs. We will visit homes near our home, and then make a small one.
intro.art: A girl kneeling on a balcony, one hand on the sunny floor and one hand under an upturned steel bucket, looking surprised.

outcomes: By the end I can name places near my home where plants and animals live: a park, a pond, a tree and under a stone.
By the end I can say what a place gives a living being: food, water, shelter and the right warmth.
By the end I can say what it is like under a stone, and who lives there.
By the end I can say that one tree or one pond is home to many living beings at once.
By the end I can guess, test, and say what I saw in my plate test.
By the end I can look at small homes gently, and put a stone back the way I found it.

terms.meaning: A habitat is the place where a living being lives. It gives them food, water and a safe place.
terms.example: A pond is a habitat for fish and frogs. The soil under a stone is a habitat for earthworms.
terms.art: Three small pictures side by side: fish and a frog in a pond, an earthworm in soil under a stone, and a crow on a nest in a tree.

terms.example: Soil under a stone is damp. A towel after your bath is damp.
terms.art: A child pressing a finger into dark, damp soil, with a small wet mark left on the finger.

terms.meaning: A shelter is a place that keeps a living being safe from the sun, the rain or danger.
terms.example: A stone is a shelter for ants. The branches of a tree are a shelter for a crow's nest.
terms.art: A flat stone with ants resting in the shade below it, while the sun shines on the ground around.

terms.meaning: A pond is a small pool of still water. Some ponds are made by nature and some by people.
terms.example: A temple tank is a pond made by people. Fish and turtles live in many temple tanks.
terms.art: A stone-stepped temple tank with fish under the water, a turtle on a step and lotus leaves on top.

explanations.concept: A habitat is a home place
explanations.definition: A habitat is the place where a living being lives. A habitat gives them food, water, shelter and the right warmth.
explanations.description: Every living being lives somewhere that gives them food, water and shelter. A fish lives in a pond, a crow in a tree and an earthworm in damp soil. Humans are animals too, and our home gives us the same things.
examples: A pond gives a fish water to swim and breathe in.
A tall tree gives a crow a high, safe place for a nest.
Your home gives you a bed, food, water and a roof against the rain.
explanations.context: This card says what a habitat is.
explanations.art: A child pointing from a pond to a tree to a stone, with a fish, a crow and an earthworm in each.

explanations.concept: Under a stone: dark, damp and cool
explanations.definition: The ground under a stone is dark, damp and cool, because the stone keeps off the sun and holds the water in.
explanations.description: The sun warms and dries open ground. A stone keeps the sun off, so the ground below stays dark and cool, and the water stays in the soil. Earthworms breathe through their skin, so it must stay damp. Pill bugs dry out fast in the sun, and ants keep their young in the dark soil.
examples: Lift a flowerpot that has stood for a week, and the floor underneath is dark and wet.
Ants often build their nest under a flat stone.
In the plate test, the soil under the plate stayed dark and damp.
explanations.context: This card says why the ground under a stone is a home for small animals.
explanations.art: A stone lifted on one side, showing dark soil with an earthworm, a curled-up pill bug and ants carrying white young, and dry pale ground in the sun around it.

explanations.concept: One tree is home to many
explanations.definition: One tree gives homes and food to many living beings at once.
explanations.description: Crows and squirrels build nests in the branches. Ants walk up the bark, and spiders spin webs between the leaves. Mynas and barbets eat the small figs of banyan and peepal trees. The tree is alive too, and her branches, bark and leaves make all these homes.
examples: A squirrel builds a nest of grass and twigs high in a mango tree.
A line of ants walks up a neem trunk.
In the Kerala monsoon, green moss covers the shady side of many trees.
explanations.context: This card says how one tree can be home to many living beings.
explanations.art: A big banyan tree with a crow's nest, a squirrel, mynas eating figs, an ant line on the trunk, a spider web and green moss on the bark.

explanations.concept: A pond is a home in water
explanations.definition: A pond is still water where water plants and water animals live.
explanations.description: Fish swim in the water and breathe with gills. Frogs lay eggs in the water, and tadpoles hatch from them. Pond skaters walk on the water without sinking. Egrets and kingfishers stand at the edge to catch fish.
examples: Tadpoles wriggle in a puddle-pond after the first monsoon rains.
A kingfisher dives into a lake in Bengaluru and comes up with a fish.
Lotus leaves float on a temple tank in Odisha.
explanations.context: This card says who lives in and around a pond.
explanations.art: A pond with fish below, tadpoles at the edge, a pond skater on top, a dragonfly above, a lotus and an egret standing in the shallows.

explanations.concept: A park has many small habitats
explanations.definition: In a park, the grass, the flowers and the soil are different habitats, each with their own living beings.
explanations.description: Grasshoppers hide in the grass, and mynas walk on the grass to catch them. Bees and butterflies drink a sweet juice called nectar from flowers. Under the grass, earthworms dig tunnels in the soil.
examples: A myna hops behind the grass cutter, picking up the insects that jump out.
A honeybee pushes into a flower to drink nectar.
After rain, small heaps of soil on the grass show where earthworms are working below.
explanations.context: This card says how one park is many homes.
explanations.art: A slice of park: a butterfly on a flower at the top, a grasshopper in the grass in the middle, and earthworm tunnels in the soil below.

explanations.concept: Do small animals choose their home?
explanations.description: Pill bugs gather under stones and pots, where it is damp and dark. Some scientists say a pill bug senses dry air and light, and chooses to look for a damp, dark place. Others say pill bugs walk fast in dry places and slow down in damp ones, so they end up together in the damp, like people slowing down at a shady bus stop.
examples: Pill bugs move quickly across a dry floor and stop under a pot.
Pill bugs rest in a damp place and walk on when the floor dries.
An earthworm on a dry path wriggles back towards the damp soil.

perspectives.explanation: Small animals sense their world and choose what to do. A pill bug senses dry air and chooses to look for damp.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study how pill bugs move
perspectives.explanation: Pill bugs walk faster and turn more in dry places, and slow down in damp places. That is enough to bring many of them together under a stone.

explanations.context: This card asks if small animals choose where they live.
explanations.art: Pill bugs crossing a dry tile floor quickly, with motion lines, and several pill bugs resting together under the edge of a flowerpot.

agreed.text: Different places near home hold different living beings.
agreed.evidence: Under a stone you find earthworms and pill bugs. In a tree you find nests and squirrels. In a pond you find fish and tadpoles. People who count living beings in a park find different kinds in the grass, the flowers and the soil.

agreed.text: Earthworms need damp skin to breathe.
agreed.evidence: An earthworm has no lungs. Oxygen passes in through the damp skin. Scientists have seen that an earthworm on dry, hot ground soon dries out and dies.
Trees on roadsides, lakes, temple tanks, cracks in walls and the soil in plant pots are all homes. Bird counts in Indian cities find many kinds of birds living right among the buildings.

challenging.claim: The small animals under stones are dirty and dangerous.
challenging.who: A common fear among children and grown-ups
challenging.for: A centipede or a scorpion can bite or sting.
challenging.against: Most animals under a stone, like earthworms, pill bugs and ants, do not hurt people. But a centipede or a scorpion can bite or sting. So look with your eyes and do not touch with bare hands.
challenging.context: This card is about a common fear: that the animals under a stone are all harmful.

challenging.claim: A pond with green water is a dead, dirty pond.
challenging.for: Green water looks dirty, and very green ponds can smell bad.
challenging.against: The green colour comes from millions of tiny living beings called algae, which many pond animals eat. But if dirty water flows in, the algae can grow too much and the fish get too little air.
challenging.context: This card is about green ponds: are they full of life, or a sign of trouble?

challenging.claim: Wild habitats are only in forests, far away from cities.
challenging.for: Big wild animals like tigers and elephants live in forests, not in towns.
challenging.against: A city tree, a lake, a crack in a wall and the soil under a pot are all wild habitats. Crows, squirrels, frogs, ants and many plants live in them without anyone looking after them.
challenging.context: This card is about a common idea: that wild homes are only far away.

big_questions.q: Why is it cooler under a stone than on top of the stone in the sun?
big_questions.hint: Think about where the sunlight lands, and where the water in the soil can go.

big_questions.q: How did a peepal tree come to grow in a crack, high up on a wall?
big_questions.hint: Who eats peepal figs? Where might that bird sit afterwards?

big_questions.q: If ants have lived under a stone for years, whose stone is it?
big_questions.hint: Who put the stone there? Who uses the stone? Does a stone belong to anyone?

big_questions.q: Your flat is your habitat. What does your home give you that a pond gives a frog?
big_questions.hint: Think about water, food, shelter and a safe place to sleep.

story.title: The Old Pot on Paati's Balcony
story.note: Kiran, Paati and Amma are made up. What the pill bug, the earthworm and the ants do in the story is true of these animals.
text: Kiran lived on the fourth floor of a building in Chennai, with his Amma and his Paati. Paati is the Tamil word for grandmother. On their balcony stood an old clay pot of jasmine.
Kiran had a new red cycle. He wanted the corner where the pot stood. "Paati, can I move the jasmine pot?" he asked.
Paati put down her tumbler of coffee. "You may," she said. "But first, let us lift it slowly and look underneath. Someone may live there."
"Under a pot?" said Kiran. "Who would live under a pot?"
Paati held the heavy pot and tipped it gently onto its side. Under it, the floor was dark and wet. A smell came up, like soil after rain. Kiran put his hand on the dark patch. "It is cold, Paati!"
Then a tiny grey creature with many legs walked across the wet patch. Kiran touched her very lightly with a leaf. At once she rolled herself up into a little ball, like a grey pea.
"That is a pill bug," said Paati. "When a pill bug feels a touch, she rolls up tight. Her hard back keeps her safe."

Near the hole at the bottom of the pot, a thin pink earthworm was stretching long and then squeezing short. At the edge of the patch, ants were rushing about. Each ant carried a small white bundle in her jaws.
"What are they carrying?" asked Kiran.
"Their young ones," said Paati. "We took off their roof. So the ants are carrying their babies to a darker place."
Kiran touched the floor out in the sun. It was hot and dry. He touched the floor where the pot had been. It was cool and damp. "Paati, it is like two different places, right next to each other."

"Yes," said Paati. "Out in the hot sun, the pill bug's body would dry up. The earthworm breathes through her skin, and her skin must stay wet. So they live where it is dark, damp and cool. The ground under our pot is just right for them."
Kiran looked down at the little grey ball. Slowly the pill bug uncurled. She walked back towards the dark patch, as fast as her many legs could go.
"Where will they all go if I move the pot?" asked Kiran.
Paati did not answer. She waited, and let Kiran think.
"I will keep my cycle in the other corner," said Kiran at last. Together they set the pot down again, very slowly, so that nobody was squashed.
That evening, Kiran found a broken floor tile in the storeroom. He filled an old pot with soil. He poured water on the soil until it was dark. Then he laid the tile flat on top, in the shady corner.
"What is that?" asked Amma, coming out with the washing.
"A new house," said Kiran. "For anybody who needs one."
The next morning, before school, Kiran lifted the tile very slowly. The soil underneath was dark and wet. Two tiny ants were already there, walking about in the damp.
"They found it already," Kiran whispered. And he put the tile back, just as gently as Paati had put back the pot.
story.epiphany: Kiran finds that the cool, dark, damp ground under a pot is a home, so moving a pot means moving someone's home.
ask: Who lived under Paati's pot? What did each one do?
How was the floor under the pot different from the floor in the sun?
Why did Kiran keep his cycle in the other corner?
art: A boy with a new red cycle on a city balcony, looking at an old clay pot of jasmine while his grandmother drinks coffee.
A grandmother tipping a clay pot on its side, showing a dark wet patch on the floor beneath.
A grey pill bug rolled into a tiny ball beside a leaf, an earthworm by the pot's drain hole, and ants carrying white young.
The boy with one hand on the sunny floor and one hand on the dark damp patch.
The boy lifting a broken tile on a pot of dark soil in the morning, with two tiny ants underneath.

games.title: Lift the Stone: a memory game of homes
games.context: This is a memory game about homes near home. The cards lie face down, like stones on the ground. You lift two at a time. If you find a living being and a place where they live, you keep both.

printables.title: 12 cards to cut out: 6 places and 6 living beings

rules: Mix the 12 cards and lay them face down on the floor in rows, like stones. Six cards are places and six are living beings.
Take turns. Lift two cards and show them to everyone. After your turn, the next player goes.
If you find a living being and a place where they live, say why they live there. Keep both cards.
Some living beings fit more than one place. Any true pair counts, if you can say why.
If the two cards do not go together, turn them face down again in the same spots.
The game ends when no cards are left, or when the cards that are left do not go together. The player with the most pairs wins. If you play as a team, count the pairs together.

setup.art: Twelve cards face down on a floor in three rows, with two children and a grown-up sitting round them.
setup.caption: 1. Lay the cards face down, like stones.

setup.art: A child lifting two cards, 'Under a stone' and 'Earthworm', and smiling.
setup.caption: 2. Lift two. Is it a living being and their home?

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 12 cards. 2. Read each card aloud once. 3. Mix them and lay them face down in rows.
flow.say: These cards are like stones on the ground. Under each one is a place, or a living being. Let's find who lives where.
flow.kid: The cards are like stones. Lift two. Find a living being and their home.

flow.do: Take turns lifting two cards. When a pair fits, ask why. If your child is unsure, give a hint from the notes below.
flow.say: You found the earthworm and the stone. Why does an earthworm live under a stone?
flow.kid: Lift two cards. Do they go together? Say why.

ask.q: Why does an earthworm live under a stone?
good: It is damp there.
The earthworm's skin needs to stay wet.
The sun cannot dry the soil there.

ask.q: Why does a squirrel build a nest high in a tree?
good: To be safe from cats and dogs.
It is high up and safe.

flow.parent: Accept any true pair with a reason. Earthworm: lives in damp soil under stones, and breathes through damp skin. Squirrel: builds a nest high in a tree, safe from cats. Tadpole: lives in a pond and grows into a frog. Grasshopper: hides and eats in the grass. Honeybee: drinks nectar from flowers. Peepal seedling: grows in a wall crack, from a seed a bird dropped. An earthworm also lives under the grass in the park.

flow.do: Count the pairs. Gather all the place cards in a row and put each living being under a home.
flow.say: Look at all the homes. Which one is the darkest and dampest?
flow.kid: Count your pairs. Which home is the darkest and dampest?

check.q: Which home is dark, damp and cool?
check.why: A stone keeps off the sun and holds the water in the soil. So the ground under it is dark, damp and cool.

games.title: Pill Bug Says: a crawling game
games.players: 1 or more children and a grown-up who calls out the places
games.context: This is a moving game. You pretend to be a pill bug, a small grey animal who lives under stones. A grown-up calls out a place. In a dry, bright place you crawl fast. In a damp, dark place you slow down and rest.

printables.title: 8 place cards for the grown-up to call out

items.f: The hot floor in the sun

items.b: Damp and dark: slow down and rest.

items.f: A dry newspaper on the balcony
Under a pile of wet leaves
items.b: Damp and dark: slow down and rest.

items.f: Under a stone in the park
items.b: Damp and dark: slow down and rest.
Roll up into a tight ball. Count to five, then uncurl.

rules: The child is a pill bug and crawls on hands and knees.
The grown-up turns over a place card and reads the front aloud.
In a dry, bright place, the pill bug crawls fast.
In a damp, dark place, the pill bug slows down and rests under the cloth.
If the card says someone touches you, the grown-up taps your shoulder. Roll up into a ball.
After all 8 cards, talk about it: were you resting in damp places or in dry places?

setup.art: A grown-up holding up a card that says 'The hot floor in the sun', while a child crawls fast on the floor.
setup.caption: 1. The grown-up reads a place. Dry and bright: crawl fast.

setup.art: A child curled up small under a table with a cloth over it, pretending to be a pill bug resting.
setup.caption: 2. Damp and dark: slow down and rest.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 8 cards and mix them. 2. Drape a cloth over a table or a chair. This is the dark resting place under a stone.
flow.say: You are a pill bug now. Your body dries out in the hot sun. Listen to each place, and move the way a pill bug would.
flow.kid: You are a pill bug. Listen to each place. Dry and bright? Crawl fast. Damp and dark? Rest.

flow.do: Read one card at a time. Wait for your child to move before you read the back.
flow.say: The hot floor in the sun! What does a pill bug do here?
flow.kid: Listen to the place. How does a pill bug move here?

ask.q: Why does a pill bug crawl fast on a dry, sunny floor?
good: The sun would dry the pill bug out.
To get to a damp place quickly.

flow.parent: Real pill bugs do this. Scientists found that they walk faster in dry places and slow down in damp ones.

flow.do: Sit together. Ask where the pill bug ended up resting.
flow.say: Where did you rest? If you crawl fast in the dry and slow in the damp, where do you end up?
flow.kid: Where did you rest most? Was it damp or dry there?
flow.think: Did the pill bug choose the damp place, or just end up there? What do you think?

check.q: Where does a pill bug spend the day?
options: Under a damp stone or pot
On top of a sunny wall
check.why: A pill bug loses water fast in dry air. Under a damp stone or pot, the pill bug's body stays moist.

experiments.title: The Plate on the Soil: what happens under a cover?
experiments.context: You wet the soil in a pot and cover half of it with a plate, like a stone. You leave the pot in the sun for about three hours. Then you look at and touch both halves.
experiments.question: After a few hours in the sun, is the soil under a plate different from the soil in the open?
experiments.predict: Guess first. After three hours, will the soil under the plate be wet or dry? And the soil in the sun? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Both halves are in the same pot, with the same soil and the same water, in the same sun, for the same time. Only one thing is different: one half has a plate on top.

materials.item: a plant pot with soil, or a wide plastic tub of soil from any pot
a flat clay or ceramic plate, a tile or a flat lid that covers about half the soil (not steel, which gets hot)
two pieces of tissue or newspaper

schedule.what: In the morning: wet the soil, cover half with a plate, guess, and put the pot in the sun.
About three hours later: look, touch and press a tissue on both halves. Say what you found.

experiments.record: Fill in the table with your child (a grown-up writes the words). Keep the two tissues next to it to compare.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results from one family in Hyderabad

setup.art: A child pouring half a cup of water slowly over the soil of a plant pot.
setup.caption: 1. Wet the soil until the top is dark.

setup.art: A flat clay plate lying on one half of the soil in a pot, on a sunny windowsill.
setup.caption: 2. Cover half with a plate. Leave the pot in the sun.

setup.art: Two tissues side by side: one with a damp brown mark, one almost clean, next to the pot with the plate lifted.
setup.caption: 3. Three hours later, press a tissue on each half.

flow.do: 1. Pour about half a cup of water slowly over the soil, until the whole top is dark and damp. 2. Let your child touch the soil. 3. Lay the plate flat on one half.
flow.say: Feel the soil. It is all wet now. This plate is like a stone. What will the soil be like under the plate in three hours? And in the sun? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Feel the wet soil. Put the plate on one half. The plate is like a stone. What will happen? Why?

ask.q: What do you think the soil under the plate will be like? Why?
good: Still wet, because the sun can't reach it.
Cool, because it's in the shade.

flow.parent: Write down your child's guess and their reason. Use a plant that can take a few hours of sun, or a tub of soil with no plant.

flow.do: Put the pot in the sunniest window or on the balcony. Look at the clock together and note the time.
flow.say: Now the sun gets to work. We will come back in three hours.
flow.kid: Put the pot in the sun. Look at the clock. We come back in three hours.
flow.wait: Leave the pot in the sun for about three hours. If there is no sun today, leave it in the brightest place until evening.

flow.do: 1. Look at the open soil first. 2. Touch it. 3. Lift the plate slowly and look under it. 4. Touch that soil. 5. Press a tissue on each half for a count of five.
flow.say: Look at the soil in the sun. Now lift the plate slowly. What do you see? Touch both halves. Which feels cooler? Which feels wetter?
flow.kid: Look at the soil in the sun. Lift the plate slowly. Touch both halves. Which is cooler? Which is wetter?

ask.q: How is the soil under the plate different from the soil in the sun?
good: It is darker.
It is wet and cool.
The tissue got a wet mark.

ask.q: Look under the plate itself. Do you see any drops of water?
good: Yes, there are little drops.
The plate is wet underneath.

flow.parent: Usually the soil under the plate is darker, wetter and cooler, and leaves a damp mark on the tissue. The soil in the sun goes pale and dry on top. Small drops may form under the plate. If the day was cloudy, the difference is smaller: leave it longer.

flow.do: Ask your child to say three things: what they think, what they saw, and why. Then look back at their guess together.
flow.say: Tell me what you found. What did you see and feel? Why do you think the plate made a difference? Was your guess right?
flow.kid: Say what you found. What did you see and feel? Why did the plate make a difference?

ask.q: Who would like to live under the plate? Who would like the soil in the sun?
good: An earthworm would like the soil under the plate.
Pill bugs and ants would live under the plate.
Nobody small would like the hot dry soil.

flow.think: A plate is not a home. But the damp, dark place under it could become one. Who might find it first?

check.q: Why did the soil under the plate stay damp?
options: The plate kept the sun off and held the water in
The plate was cold from the fridge
check.why: The plate blocked the sunlight, and the water in the soil could not escape into the air so quickly. The soil in the open dried in the sun.

activities.title: Feel the Places: damp or dry, dark or bright, cool or warm?
activities.context: In this activity you visit five places in your home and touch each one. You decide if each place is damp or dry, dark or bright, and cool or warm. Then you think about who might like to live there.

schedule.what: Touch five places in the home. Mark each one. Say who might live there.

activities.record: A table of the five places, with a sun or a moon for bright or dark, and a drop for damp.

setup.art: A child touching a sunny windowsill with one hand.
setup.caption: 1. Touch a sunny windowsill.

setup.art: A child shining a torch under a kitchen sink and touching the floor there.
setup.caption: 2. Touch the floor under the kitchen sink.

setup.art: A simple table with five places, and a sun, a moon and a water drop drawn for each.
setup.caption: 3. Mark each place: bright or dark, damp or dry.

flow.do: Visit five places with your child. Try a sunny windowsill, under the kitchen sink and under the doormat. Then try a corner of the bathroom floor and the soil in a plant pot. Your child touches each one.
flow.say: Touch this place. Is it damp or dry? Is it dark or bright? Is it cool or warm?
flow.kid: Touch each place. Damp or dry? Dark or bright? Cool or warm?
flow.parent: Draw a sun or a moon for bright or dark, and a drop for damp.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask which place a pill bug would choose, and which place a sunbathing lizard would choose.
flow.say: A pill bug needs damp and dark. A garden lizard likes to warm up in the sun. Which place would each one choose?
flow.kid: Which place would a pill bug like? Which place would a lizard in the sun like?

ask.q: Which place in our home is most like the ground under a stone?
good: Under the doormat.
Under the sink, because it is dark and damp.

flow.think: Our home has many small places. Could each one be home to someone different?

activities.safety: Under the kitchen sink, touch only the floor. Keep away from the cleaning bottles.

activities.title: One Tree, Many Homes (if a tree is near)
activities.context: If you can see a tree from your window, or pass one on a walk, this activity is for you. You watch one tree for ten minutes and tick every living being and every home you find on it.

materials.item: a tick card (a grown-up draws it): a nest, a bird, a squirrel, an ant, a spider web, a hole, a bitten leaf, moss and fruit

schedule.what: Watch one tree for ten minutes. Tick everything you find. Talk about it.

activities.record: Your ticked card, and a drawing of your tree with every home you found.

setup.art: A girl and a grown-up standing near a neem tree, the girl holding a card with small drawings to tick.
setup.caption: 1. Stand near one tree with your tick card.

setup.art: Close-ups of a neem trunk: an ant line, a spider web, a hole in the bark and green moss.
setup.caption: 2. Look high, look at the bark, look at the roots.

flow.do: Stand with your child near one tree, or at a window that looks at a tree. Look at the top branches, then the trunk and bark, then the roots. Tick each thing you find.
flow.say: Let's look at this one tree, from the top to the bottom. Who lives here? Who comes to visit?
flow.kid: Look at the top of the tree. Look at the bark. Look at the roots. Tick what you find.
flow.parent: Neem, peepal, banyan, mango, coconut and gulmohar trees are all good. Look, and don't touch ant lines, because some ants bite.

flow.do: Count the ticks together. Ask which homes were high up and which were low down.
flow.say: How many different living beings did we find on one tree? Which ones lived high up? Which lived down low?
flow.kid: Count your ticks. Who lived high up? Who lived low down?

ask.q: Is the tree a living being too?
good: Yes, the tree is alive.
Yes, the tree grows and drinks water.

flow.think: If this tree was cut down, where would all these living beings go?

activities.title: Plants in the Cracks
activities.context: In this activity you look for small plants growing in cracks: in walls, on steps, at the edge of the building or beside a drain. You notice whether the crack is sunny or shady, and you think about how the seed got there.

schedule.what: Find plants growing in cracks near home. Draw one. Say how the seed got there.

activities.record: A drawing of one plant in a crack, with the sun or the shade drawn beside it.

setup.art: A small peepal sapling with heart-shaped leaves growing out of a crack in an old wall.
setup.caption: 1. Look for small plants growing in cracks.

setup.art: Green moss and a tiny fern in a shady, damp corner at the bottom of a wall.
setup.caption: 2. Is the crack sunny or shady? Damp or dry?

flow.do: Walk slowly with your child round the building, the staircase or the compound wall. Look in cracks for small plants, moss and grass.
flow.say: Plants can live in very small places. Let's find plants growing in cracks. Is this crack sunny or shady?
flow.kid: Find a plant growing in a crack. Is the crack sunny or shady?
flow.parent: Peepal and banyan seedlings, small ferns, moss and grass are common finds. Moss grows most on damp, shady walls.

flow.do: Ask how a seed got into a crack so high. Then your child draws one plant in their crack.
flow.say: Birds eat the small figs of peepal and banyan trees. The seeds come out in their droppings. How could a seed get into a crack high on a wall?
flow.kid: How did a seed get into this crack? Draw the plant that grows in this crack.

ask.q: How could a peepal seed get into a crack high on a wall?
good: A bird ate a fig and dropped the seed there.
In the bird's droppings.

flow.think: A crack has only a little soil. What does the plant find there that they need?

activities.title: Pond Watch (if you pass a pond, a lake or a temple tank)
activities.context: If you pass a pond, a lake or a temple tank, this activity is for you. You stand back from the edge and watch for ten minutes. You look for living beings in the water, on top of the water, and in the air above it.

materials.item: a tick card (a grown-up draws it): a fish, a frog, a tadpole, a lotus, a dragonfly, a pond skater, an egret and a duck

activities.safety: Stay well back from the edge and hold a grown-up's hand. Do not lean over the water or go down slippery steps.

schedule.what: Watch a pond from a safe spot. Tick what you see. Talk about it.

activities.record: Your ticked card, and a drawing of the pond in three layers: under the water, on top, and in the air.

setup.art: A grown-up and a child standing back from the edge of a temple tank, looking at fish and lotus leaves.
setup.caption: 1. Stand back from the edge with a grown-up.

setup.art: A pond drawn in three layers: fish under the water, a pond skater on top and a dragonfly in the air.
setup.caption: 2. Look under the water, on top, and in the air above.

flow.do: Stand with your child well back from the edge. Look under the water first, then on top, then in the air above. Tick what you see.
flow.say: Let's look under the water first. Now look on top of the water. Now look in the air. Who lives here?
flow.kid: Look under the water. Look on top. Look in the air. Who lives here?
flow.parent: Fish, tadpoles, pond skaters, dragonflies, lotus or water lilies, egrets and ducks are common.

flow.do: Count the ticks together. Ask which beings live in the water all the time, and which only come to visit.
flow.say: Who lives in the water all the time? Who only comes to visit?
flow.kid: Who lives in the water all the time? Who only visits?

ask.q: Why does an egret come to the pond?
good: To catch fish.
To find food.

flow.think: Without the pond, where would the fish and the tadpoles live?

projects.title: A Stone Home on the Balcony
projects.context: In this three-day project you make a small damp, dark place with a tile on soil, like a stone. Each morning you lift the tile slowly to see if anyone has moved in. Then you put the tile back gently.

materials.item: a plant pot, a tray or a bowl of soil
a flat tile, a clay pot piece or a flat stone

schedule.what: Wet the soil. Lay the tile flat on it in a shady corner of the balcony or a window ledge inside the grill.
Lift the tile slowly. Look, count and draw. Put it back gently.
Lift the tile again. Look, count and draw. Compare with yesterday.

projects.record: A drawing for each morning of what you found under the tile, with a tally of any ants or other small animals.

setup.art: A child laying a flat tile on damp soil in a pot in a shady corner of a balcony.
setup.caption: 1. Lay a tile on damp soil in a shady corner.

setup.art: A child lifting the tile slowly in the morning, and looking at ants on the dark soil.
setup.caption: 2. Each morning, lift slowly, look, and put it back.

flow.do: 1. Pour water on the soil until it is dark. 2. Lay the tile flat on top. 3. Put it in a shady corner, out of reach of pets.
flow.say: We are making a stone home. Small animals look for dark, damp places. Let's see who finds this one.
flow.kid: Wet the soil. Lay the tile flat on top. This is a stone home.

ask.q: Who do you think might come? Why?
good: Ants, because there are ants on the balcony.
A pill bug, because they like damp places.

flow.do: Lift the tile slowly. Look, count and draw what you see. Put the tile back gently, the same way.
flow.say: Lift it slowly. Is the soil still damp? Has anyone moved in? Let's count them.
flow.kid: Lift the tile slowly. Is anyone there? Count them. Put the tile back gently.
flow.parent: Ants come most often. If nobody has come, that is a result too. Keep the soil damp with a little water.

flow.do: Lift the tile again. Count and draw. Compare with yesterday's drawing.
flow.say: Are there more today, or fewer, or the same? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Count again. More, fewer or the same as yesterday? Why?
flow.think: When we stop the project, should we leave the stone home there?
flow.parent: Put the tile back the same way.

projects.safety: A grown-up lifts the tile and keeps fingers out from under it, in case of a centipede or a scorpion.

challenges.title: Make a Water Place for Birds on a Hot Day
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. In the hot months, birds in the city find it hard to get water. You design a small, safe water place for birds on your balcony or window ledge.
challenges.problem: Make a place where small birds can drink and bathe safely on a hot day, using things from home.
constraints: The water must be shallow, no deeper than the first knuckle of your finger, so small birds can stand in it.
It must be in the shade, so the water stays cool.
It must be safe from cats, and not fall off a ledge.
The water must be changed every day, so mosquitoes cannot lay eggs in it.
materials: a shallow clay plate, a steel plate or a wide lid
a stone or a tile to stand in the middle
general: A wide, shallow clay or steel plate filled with a little water.
Put it in a shady spot where you can see it from inside.
creative: Put a flat stone in the middle, so the smallest birds have somewhere to stand.
Put the plate on a high shelf inside the grill, where cats cannot reach.
Put a plant pot beside the water, so birds have a place to rest before they drink.
challenges.your_turn: Draw your water place. Put it out, and watch for two days. Who came? Which birds drank, and which bathed?

setup.art: A shallow clay plate of water with a flat stone in the middle, in the shade of a balcony plant.
setup.caption: 1. A shallow plate of water, in the shade.

setup.art: A sparrow standing on the stone in the plate, dipping her beak, while a child watches from inside the window.
setup.caption: 2. Watch from inside. Who comes to drink?

flow.do: Talk about the problem. Look at the balcony or window ledge together. Find a shady, safe spot.
flow.say: Birds need water on hot days. Where could a small bird drink safely here? What would keep the water cool?
flow.kid: Birds need water on hot days. Where could a bird drink safely?

flow.do: Your child chooses a plate and a stone and sets them up. Pour in water no deeper than a finger.
flow.say: Why should the water be shallow? Why should it be in the shade?
flow.kid: Choose a plate. Put a stone in the middle. Pour in a little water.
flow.parent: Place it where it cannot fall from a height. Change the water every day.

flow.wait: Watch over the next two days.
flow.do: Watch from inside for a few minutes at different times. Note which birds come.
flow.say: Who came to our water place? Did they drink, or did they bathe?
flow.kid: Watch from inside. Who came? Did they drink or bathe?
flow.think: We made a small new habitat. What else could we add to it?

items.p: Draw a line from each living being to their home.
items.why: Earthworms need damp soil, tadpoles need water, squirrels nest high in trees, and bees drink nectar from flowers.
items.art: An earthworm, a tadpole, a squirrel and a bee on the left; a stone, a pond, a tree and flowers on the right.

items.p: Colour the damp, dark places blue. Colour the dry, bright places yellow.
items: under a pile of wet leaves
a sandy path in the sun
items.why: A cover keeps off the sun and holds the water in, so the places under a stone, a pot or leaves stay damp and dark.
items.art: Six small pictures: a stone, a windowsill in sun, a flowerpot, a road with a hot sun, a pile of wet leaves and a sandy path.

items.p: Draw the soil from your plate test. Colour the wet soil dark brown and the dry soil pale.
items.a: The half that was under the plate is coloured dark. The half in the sun is pale.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the two halves different, as the child saw: dark and damp under the plate, pale and dry in the sun.
items.art: An empty circle for the top of a plant pot, split in half by a dotted line.

items.p: Count the animals in this picture of a tree: a crow on a nest, two squirrels, three ants on the bark, and a kite string caught in the branches.
items.why: One crow, two squirrels and three ants make 6 animals. The kite string was never alive. The tree is alive too, but the tree is a plant.
items.art: A tree with a crow on a nest, two squirrels, three ants on the bark and a kite string caught in a branch.

items.p: Write or draw one living being who lives in each place.
a: pond: a fish, a frog, a tadpole or a lotus
tree: a crow, a squirrel or ants
under a stone: an earthworm, a pill bug or ants
items.why: Any living being who really lives in that place is right. A strong answer can say what the place gives them.
items.art: Three boxes with a pond, a tree and a stone, each with an empty space underneath.

items.p: Say it to a grown-up, who writes it down: why does an earthworm live under a stone, and not on the hot road?
items.a: Under the stone the soil is damp and cool. The earthworm breathes through damp skin, and the hot road would dry the skin.
items.why: A strong answer links the place (damp and cool) to what the earthworm needs (damp skin to breathe).

items.p: Two friends in Kochi find a big flat stone in the park.

views.says: Let's lift the stone and see who lives underneath.
Let's leave the stone alone. Lifting the stone takes the roof off someone's home.

items.ask: Which friend do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other friend has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and gives a reason, such as 'Anu, because we can learn who lives there.' Then it is fair to the other side: Fathima is right that the stone is a roof for the animals.
items.why: Both friends have a point. Looking teaches us about small homes. Lifting the stone slowly, not touching, and putting the stone back the same way keeps the home safe.

items.p: Which place is the odd one out? Think about water.
items.why: A pond, a temple tank and a puddle all hold water, so water animals can live in them. A sunny windowsill is dry.

items.p: An earthworm likes to lie on hot, dry ground.
items.why: False. An earthworm breathes through her skin, and her skin must stay damp. Hot, dry ground would dry her out.

items.p: Which place gives a crow a high, safe home for her nest?
items.why: A crow builds her nest in the branches of a tall tree, high above cats and dogs.

items.p: Lakshmi, a girl in Class 1, lays a tile on damp soil in a sunny pot. After lunch, she lifts the tile. What will she most likely find?
items.why: The tile keeps off the sun and holds the water in, just like the plate in our test. Dry, pale soil is what the open half looks like.

items.p: Put the plate test in order.
items: Lift the plate and touch both halves
Leave the pot in the sun
Put the plate on half the soil
a: Put the plate on half the soil
Leave the pot in the sun
Lift the plate and touch both halves
items.why: First we wet the soil, then cover half, then wait in the sun, then look and touch.

items.p: Draw a tree. Draw three different homes on your tree: one high up, one on the bark and one near the roots.
items.a: For example, a crow's nest high up, ants on the bark, and an earthworm or a pill bug in the soil at the roots.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that one tree holds different homes at different heights.
items.art: An outline of a tree with empty space at the top, on the trunk and at the roots.

items.p: Say it to a grown-up, who writes it down: on a hot afternoon, do you sit in the sun or under a tree? How is that like a pill bug under a stone?
items.a: Under a tree, where the shade is cool. A pill bug goes under a stone because it is cooler and damper there.
items.why: A strong answer sees that humans and other animals both look for a shady, cool place when the sun is hot.

items.p: A pond is a home only for fish.
items.why: False. Frogs, tadpoles, pond skaters, young dragonflies, snails, lotus and many tiny beings live in a pond too.

items.p: Draw a line from each place to what the place gives.
pairs: A high, safe place for a nest
A damp, dark place to hide
items.why: Every habitat gives the living beings there something they need: shelter, damp, food or water.
items.art: A tree, a stone, a flower and a pond on the left, and small pictures of a nest, a hiding pill bug, nectar and a swimming fish on the right.

items.p: Ritu and Deepa, two sisters in Pune, watch pill bugs under a flowerpot.

views.says: The pill bugs chose this damp place. They can feel where it is nice.
The pill bugs just walked fast on the dry floor and slowly in the damp. So they ended up here.

items.ask: Which sister do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other sister has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason, such as 'Ritu, because the pill bugs sense the damp.' Then it is fair to the other side: Deepa is right that pill bugs really do walk faster in dry places.
items.why: Scientists still describe this in both ways. Pill bugs sense dry and damp, and they also walk faster in the dry. Both sisters are using real evidence.

items.p: Sort these living beings: do they live in water or on land?
items.why: Fish, tadpoles and lotus live in water. Squirrels, earthworms and grasshoppers live on land, though earthworms need damp soil.
items.art: Six small pictures: a fish, a squirrel, a tadpole, an earthworm, a lotus and a grasshopper.

items.p: This is a picture of a pond. Write the names (a grown-up can help with spelling): lotus, fish, frog, dragonfly.
a: lotus: on top of the water
items.why: A pond has homes in layers: under the water, on top of it, at the edge and in the air above.
items.art: A pond with a lotus on top, a fish under the water, a frog at the edge and a dragonfly in the air, each with an empty label line.

items.p: A pill bug is an insect, like an ant.
items.why: False. A pill bug has 14 legs, and an insect has 6. Pill bugs are cousins of crabs and prawns, not of ants.

videos.title: Roly poly (pill bug) close up: A close-up look at pill bugs and how they roll into a ball.
videos.why: Shows a pill bug up close and how it rolls into a ball, which a child may never see up close.
videos.check: Found by search: "Roly Polies Came From the Sea to Conquer the Earth" by Deep Look, 3 minutes, 30 seconds. A parent may preview it.

videos.title: Earthworms: how worms move and live in soil
videos.why: Shows how earthworms live and move through soil.
videos.check: Found by search: "Worms Are Wonderful" by SciShow Kids, 4 minutes, 34 seconds. A parent may preview it.

videos.title: Who lives at the pond?
videos.channel: Dr. Seuss (The Lorax Nature Keepers Club)
videos.why: Shows the living beings that live in and around a pond.
videos.check: Found by search: "Who Lives at the Pond? Let's Find Out!" by Dr. Seuss (The Lorax Nature Keepers Club), 3 minutes, 8 seconds. A parent may preview it.

quiz.p: Which of these is a habitat, a home place for living beings?
quiz.why: A pond is a habitat. Fish, frogs and lotus live there. A spoon and a pencil are not homes for anyone.

quiz.p: Where would you look for earthworms?
quiz.why: Earthworms need damp soil to keep their skin wet. A hot road or a dry windowsill would dry them out.

quiz.p: What is the ground under a stone like?
quiz.why: The stone keeps off the sun and holds the water in. So the ground below is dark, damp and cool.
Tadpoles hatch from frog eggs in the water and live there until they grow into frogs.

quiz.p: Who lives in one big tree?
opts: Many beings: birds, squirrels, ants and more
quiz.why: One tree is home to many living beings at once, high in the branches, on the bark and in the leaves.

quiz.p: Why do bees visit the flowers in a park?
quiz.why: Flowers make a sweet juice called nectar. Bees and butterflies drink it.

quiz.p: In the plate test, which soil was cooler to touch?
opts: The soil in the open sun
quiz.why: The plate kept the sun off the soil under it, so that soil stayed cooler. The soil in the open sun warmed up and dried.

quiz.p: You lift a stone in the park and find ants and a pill bug. What should you do next?
opts: Put the stone back gently, the same way
Take the pill bug home in your pocket
quiz.why: The stone is their roof. Putting the stone back gently gives them their damp, dark home again.

quiz.p: Why does a squirrel build a nest high in a tree?
opts: To be safe from cats and dogs
Because the ground is too wet
quiz.why: High branches keep a squirrel's babies away from cats, dogs and other animals on the ground.

quiz.p: Paati's ants carried their white young away when she tipped the pot. Why?
opts: The young ones need a dark place, and the pot's roof was gone
The young ones wanted to see the sun
The ants were tidying the floor
quiz.why: Ant young ones are kept in the dark and damp. When the pot was lifted, the ants moved them to a darker place.

applications: Gardeners lift pots and stones to check for earthworms, which are a sign of healthy soil.
Cities that keep their lakes, ponds and old trees keep homes for birds, frogs and fish.
Scientists and families count the living beings in one park or one tree to see how a place is changing.
People put out shallow water for birds in the hot months, making a small new habitat on a balcony.

spotted.text: Fish and turtles living in a temple tank, in towns across Tamil Nadu and Kerala.
spotted.art: A temple tank with stone steps, fish under the water and a turtle resting on a step.

spotted.text: A small peepal tree growing out of an old wall or a roof, in almost any Indian town.
spotted.art: A peepal sapling with heart-shaped leaves growing from the top of an old wall.

spotted.text: Green moss on walls and tree trunks during the Kerala and Konkan monsoon.
spotted.art: A wet compound wall covered in bright green moss in the rain.

spotted.text: Egrets walking beside cows in a field, catching the insects the cows stir up, from Assam to Karnataka.
spotted.art: A white egret walking beside a grazing cow in a green field.

spotted.text: Lotus leaves covering a village pond in Odisha or West Bengal.
spotted.art: A pond covered in round lotus leaves, with one pink lotus flower.

open_questions.q: How many kinds of living beings live in one handful of soil?
open_questions.why_open: A handful of soil holds millions of tiny beings. Most of the kinds have never been named, so nobody knows the full count.

open_questions.q: Why do so many earthworms come up out of the soil when it rains?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists still argue. Some think wet ground lets them travel far. Others think the sound of rain, or too little air in the wet soil, sends them up.

open_questions.q: What does a pill bug sense and feel when the stone above them is lifted?
open_questions.why_open: Pill bugs sense light, touch and damp. What that is like from inside a pill bug, nobody knows.

ask_kids: Which place near our home is the dampest? Who might live there?
If you were a pill bug, where in our flat would you hide?
How many living beings can you see on the nearest tree?
Where does the water go when a puddle dries up? Who lived in the puddle?
Is our flat a habitat? What does it give us?

jokes.j: Why did the earthworm stay under the stone all day?
jokes.a: Because the sun was too hot to handle, and the earthworm has no hands!

jokes.j: What did the pill bug say when someone tapped her?
jokes.a: Nothing. She was all wrapped up!

jokes.j: What is a squirrel's favourite house?
Why did the ant move under the plate?
jokes.a: The ant heard the rent was free!

jokes.j: Why are frogs always so happy?
Why do frogs love the pond?
jokes.a: It has the best lily-pad flats!

jokes.j: What did the stone say to the earthworm?
Why do bees have sticky hair?

maths.problem: In the plate test, Selvi, a girl in Class 1, put the plate on the soil at 9 o'clock. She lifted the plate at 12 o'clock. How many hours did the plate stay on?
maths.explain: From 9 to 10 is one hour, 10 to 11 is two, and 11 to 12 is three. So the plate stayed on for 3 hours.
maths.context: This is about the plate test, where you covered half the soil and left the pot in the sun.
maths.why_maths: Knowing how long the plate stayed on lets us compare our test with a friend's, and try a longer or shorter time.

maths.problem: Revathi, a girl in Class 1, counted small plants growing in wall cracks. She found 4 on the shady wall and 1 on the sunny wall. Which wall had more plants? Why might that be?
maths.answer: The shady wall had more plants, 4 instead of 1.
maths.explain: 4 is more than 1. A shady wall stays damp for longer after rain, so small plants and moss can live there more easily.
maths.context: This is about looking for plants growing in cracks near home.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the two counts shows a pattern, and the pattern makes us ask why shade helps plants in cracks.

maths.problem: Mahi, a girl in Class 1, laid a tile on damp soil on day 1. On day 2 she lifted it and found 2 ants. On day 3 she found 5 ants. Which day had more ants? What is happening to the number?
maths.answer: Day 3 had more ants, 5. The number is going up.
maths.explain: 2, then 5: there were more ants on day 3 than on day 2. More ants were finding the damp, dark place.
maths.context: This is about the stone home project, where you lifted a tile each morning to see who had moved in.
maths.why_maths: Writing the counts in order shows whether the stone home is filling up, which one look alone cannot tell us.

links.why: For the parent: photograph a small animal or plant near home and find out their name.

links.title: Lalbagh Botanical Garden
links.why: Old trees, a lake and lawns in the middle of the city, each with their own birds and insects.

links.why: A big natural lake at the edge of the city, home to fish, water plants and many birds.

links.why: A forest with streams and lakes inside a big city.

warmup.q: Name one place near home where living beings live.
warmup.a: A tree, a pond, a park, or under a stone.

warmup.q: Is the ground under a stone damp or dry?
warmup.a: Damp, and dark and cool too.
Fish, frogs, tadpoles, lotus and more.

warmup.q: Why does an earthworm need damp soil?
warmup.a: An earthworm breathes through damp skin.

warmup.q: What does a pill bug do when touched?
warmup.a: She rolls up into a tight ball.
The place where a living being lives and finds what they need.

founder: ideas/by_topic/habitats-and-adaptation.md: the concept activities are about oceans, the atmosphere and the monsoon, which fit higher levels. The SCI Cards (Rachel Carson, Marie Tharp, Aditi Pant, M. S. Swaminathan) were not used at this level.
Cambridge Stage 1, 1.2 Local environments: where living things live and why; plants growing in cracks.
science: Earthworms have no lungs and exchange gases through a moist skin; they die if the skin dries (any invertebrate zoology text).

Woodlice lose water quickly through their cuticle and gather in humid, dark places. Their speed and turning rate rise in dry air (humidity kinesis: Gunn, 1937, Journal of Experimental Biology). Pill bugs (Armadillidiidae) roll into a ball when disturbed.
Ants move their larvae and pupae to safety when the nest is disturbed.
Peepal and banyan (Ficus) seeds are spread by birds and bats that eat the figs; seedlings often grow on walls and buildings.
Water striders (pond skaters) stand on the surface film; dragonfly nymphs live underwater for months or years.

Maria Sibylla Merian (1647-1717): began raising silkworms at 13; published Der Raupen wunderbare Verwandlung (1679), showing insects with their food plants and life stages; went to Suriname in 1699 with her daughter Dorothea; Metamorphosis insectorum Surinamensium (1705).
Tolkappiyam, Porulatikaram, Akattinaiyiyal: the landscapes (tinai) and their native elements (karupporul), such as plants, birds and animals.

Acharanga Sutra, Book 1, Lecture 4, Lesson 1 (Jacobi translation): all breathing, existing, living, sentient creatures should not be slain, nor treated with violence, nor abused, nor tormented, nor driven away.
Why earthworms surface after rain is unsettled: migration while the ground is wet, response to rain vibrations, and low oxygen in waterlogged soil have all been proposed.
Bird baths: shallow water in shade, changed daily to stop mosquito breeding.

roots.context: We have looked at homes near our home, and made a damp, dark place with a plate. Now we ask what that tells us about places and the beings who live in them.

deep_truth.truth: We covered half of some wet soil with a plate and left it in the sun for three hours. Under the plate, the soil stayed dark, damp and cool. In the open, the same soil turned pale and dry. So a flat cover makes a new place, where animals that need damp can live.
deep_truth.habit: We think of a home as a big place, like a forest or a pond. But a home can be as small as the ground under one stone.
deep_truth.evidence: In the plate test, the same soil, the same water and the same sun gave two different places a hand apart. Only the plate was different.

three.who_am_i: You are an animal who looks for a cool, shady place on a hot day, just as a pill bug does under a stone.
three.what_is_life: Every living being needs a place that gives them food, water and safety. Life finds such places everywhere, even under a pot.
three.what_is_this_world: The world near your home is made of many small homes side by side: a tree, a puddle, a crack, a stone.

roots.thread: The same sun and rain fall on all the ground near your home. A stone, a tree or a pond changes how much light, water and warmth reach one spot. So each spot gives different living beings what they need.

teachings.teaching: The Tolkappiyam is a very old Tamil book about language and poems. It sorts the land into kinds, such as hills, forest, farmland and seashore. Each kind of land has its own trees, flowers, birds and animals.
teachings.link: Our plate test found two different homes a hand apart. The Tolkappiyam saw the same thing across a whole country: each kind of place has its own living beings.

teachings.teaching: This old Jain teaching says that no breathing, living being should be killed, hurt or driven away. Many Jain monks and nuns carry a soft brush to move tiny beings gently out of their path.
teachings.link: When we lift a stone, the beings underneath lose their roof. Putting the stone back gently gives them their home again.

science.text: Earthworms breathe through their skin, and their skin must stay damp. Pill bugs lose water fast in dry air. So both live where the ground stays damp.
A handful of soil holds millions of tiny living beings, and most of their kinds have never been named.

other_view.who: Scientists who study how pill bugs move
other_view.view: These scientists say pill bugs simply walk fast and turn often in dry, bright places, and slow down in damp, dark ones. So many pill bugs end up together under a stone, without needing to decide anything.

practice.title: A small dark home
practice.say: Sit comfortably. Cup your hands and cover your eyes, without pressing. See how dark it is inside. Breathe in slowly and out slowly, three times. Feel how warm and still it is in there. Now open your hands slowly, and let the light come in. Your hands made a small, dark home, just as a stone does for an earthworm.
practice.kid: Cover your eyes with cupped hands. See the dark. Breathe slowly three times. Open your hands slowly. Your hands made a dark home, like a stone.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out where small creatures like caterpillars come from, and where they live? This card tells the true story of a woman who watched them closely.
how_we_found_out.story: About 350 years ago, in Germany, many people believed that small creatures like caterpillars and worms grew out of mud, dew or rotting things, all by themselves. A girl called Maria Sibylla Merian wanted to see for herself. When she was 13, she began to raise silkworms and other caterpillars at home. She fed them, watched them every day and drew them. She saw each caterpillar eat and grow, and then make a hard case called a pupa. Later a moth or a butterfly came out. She also saw that many kinds of caterpillar eat only certain plants. So she painted insects on the plants they eat, with the eggs, the caterpillar, the pupa and the grown insect in one picture. In 1679 she published a book of these paintings. Twenty years later, at the age of 52, she sailed to Suriname in South America with her daughter Dorothea, to study the insects and plants there. Her pictures showed that each small creature has a life story and a home plant.
how_we_found_out.who: Maria Sibylla Merian, a German artist and naturalist, with her daughter Dorothea
how_we_found_out.when: From about 1660 (her first silkworms) to 1705 (her book on the insects of Suriname)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That caterpillars and other small creatures grew out of mud, dew or rotting things by themselves. Merian raised them from eggs, watched every stage, and showed them living and feeding on the plants they eat.
how_we_found_out.art: A woman in a long dress of the 1600s at a table, painting a caterpillar and a butterfly on a leafy branch, with a box of caterpillars on leaves beside her.
